Active power in kW equals apparent power in kVA multiplied by the power factor. For modern UPS with an output PF of 1.0 the figures coincide: 20 kVA equals 20 kW. For a load with PF 0.9: 20 kVA equals 18 kW. Diesel generators use cos φ 0.8: 100 kVA equals 80 kW. When selecting, check both values: the UPS must pass on both kVA and kW.

We divide the active power in kW by the load power factor and add a margin for growth. Rating: the next standard value up from the series 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, 100 … 1200 kVA. For N+1 modular systems we add one 25 or 50 kVA module.

General-purpose 12 V AGM batteries last 3–5 years in real operation; long-life series (Ritar RA, EnerGrid FT, BAE Secura 12V) are rated for 10–12 years at 20–25 °C. 2 V OPzV and OPzS cells last 15–20 years. Every 10 °C above 25 °C roughly halves the service life, so the battery room needs air conditioning and testing every six months.

The second parameter is battery runtime. For sites with a diesel generator 10–15 minutes is enough for the generator to start and take the load. Without a generator, 30–60 minutes are allowed for a controlled shutdown or switchover to a backup feed. The number of blocks in a battery string is set by the UPS bus voltage, and the capacity is calculated from the energy to be delivered over that time, taking into account inverter efficiency and the fact that a battery delivers less than its nominal capacity in a short discharge. Battery autonomy above two hours is rarely justified: a generator plus a UPS with 15–30 minutes is cheaper and more reliable.

Load grows over time: servers, machines and air conditioners are added. A UPS should not run constantly at 100 % of its rating: this affects the life of capacitors and fans, overload capacity for inrush currents and operation at reduced mains voltage. 20–30 % is considered a typical engineering margin; for sites with a precisely known and constant load, 10–20 % is enough.

Selecting an uninterruptible power supply starts with the load. Add up the active power of all equipment that must keep running when the mains fail, in kW, convert to kVA using the power factor and add a 20–30 % margin for growth and inrush currents. This figure determines the UPS rating from the standard series, and the number of phases depends on the power: up to 10 kVA usually single-phase rack and tower models, from 10 kVA three-phase with external battery cabinets. The calculator above does this automatically and immediately shows Salicru, Kehua and Tescom models from the AEC catalogue.

We multiply the apparent load power by 1.3 (30 % margin) and by a correction for the lower input voltage limit: 1.2 at ±20 %, 1.4 for dips down to 150 V. Electromechanical type for inrush currents, electronic for sensitive electronics.
